narrative.text: By dawn, the Sarenka works has gone silent for the first time since the rescue eighteen months ago. Not sabotage this time. Not a collapse. The men simply did not go down the shaft, and by mid-morning three more collieries across Kravenstal have followed them into stillness.

Chancellor, this isn't spontaneous. Every foreman I've spoken to says the same thing — wages, hours, the usual grievances, yes, but the timing is coordinated across four separate companies that have never coordinated anything in their history. Someone organized this in one week, and organizing that fast costs money nobody on that picket line has.

Four companies. Four owners who have spent thirty years undercutting each other on every contract in the province, suddenly moving in the same direction on the same morning. I have seen this arithmetic before, in smaller rooms, and it never once meant good news.
By afternoon your suspicion has a name and a face. Stefan Morvec requests an audience — not by letter this time. In person, unannounced, the first time he has come to you rather than sent a courier.

Chancellor, I will not waste your afternoon pretending surprise. The mine owners are frightened. Wage demands they cannot meet without ruin, a government they no longer trust to protect their contracts, and no confidence the Assembly will act before the whole province burns down around everyone's ears. Frightened men make arrangements with each other. I did not organize this. I did not need to.

He did not need to. That is somehow worse than if he had. It means the thing I built my career opposing — men with capital simply agreeing, quietly, to starve out anyone who threatens them — no longer needs Morvec's hand on it at all. It has become the water they swim in.

I can end this by Thursday, Chancellor. A word from me to the right four men, and the collieries reopen. Or you can manage it yourself, through the Ministry, through the Assembly, through whatever channels a government prefers to use — and discover exactly how long four idle mines can hold a province's patience.

choices.text: Let him end it. Whatever this costs later, forty thousand idle miners cannot wait on your channels to work faster than his word does.
Refuse him. Send the Labor Ministry to mediate directly with the miners' representatives — slower, and entirely the government's own doing.
Do neither, for now. Tell Morvec you need until Thursday to decide whether a mediated peace serves Kravenstal better than his quiet arrangement — and mean it.

narrative.text: By Thursday, exactly as promised, the collieries reopen. The wage increase granted is smaller than the miners asked for and larger than the owners wanted, a number that satisfies precisely no one and ends precisely the strike.

I have just watched a private citizen resolve a labor crisis across four companies faster than my own government could convene a committee to discuss convening a committee. I do not know yet what that costs me. I suspect I will find out at a time of his choosing, not mine.

The mediation drags into its second week before the first colliery reaches terms. Marić does not sleep much during it. Neither, by his account, do the men on the picket lines, who have taken to calling the standoff by his name rather than the mine's.
It is slower. It is also, when it finally settles, entirely mine to answer for — not a favor owed to a man who does not forget favors owed. I find I can live with slow.

Thursday arrives with no decision made, which Morvec receives with the particular patience of a man who has never once needed to raise his voice to get what he wants. The mines remain idle a fifth day, then a sixth.
I bought time. I am not entirely certain, watching the province hold its breath, that time was the thing worth buying.
